title: Federated Learning
shortDefinition: A machine learning approach that trains a model across distributed devices without centralizing raw data.
definition: Federated learning is a machine learning approach where a model is trained across multiple distributed devices or data sources — each holding its own local data — without that raw data ever being centralized or transmitted to a single location. Instead of moving data to a central server for training, federated learning moves the model training process to where the data already lives, sharing only model updates (not raw data) back to a coordinating server.

sections.title: How federated learning works
sections.description: A central server distributes a model to participants, who train locally and share only model updates, not raw data.

content.text: In a federated learning setup, a central server distributes a model to participating devices or data holders (which might be mobile phones, hospital systems, or other distributed data sources). Each participant trains the model locally on its own data, then sends only the resulting model parameter updates — not the raw underlying data itself — back to the central server, which aggregates these updates across all participants to improve a shared global model. This process repeats iteratively, with the model improving across rounds while raw data never leaves its original location.

items: Central server — distributes model and aggregates updates.
Participants — train model locally on their own data.
Model updates — only parameters are shared, not raw data.
Aggregation — server combines updates across participants.
Iterative rounds — model improves while data stays local.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Federated learning moves the training process to where the data lives — raw data never leaves its original location.

sections.title: Why federated learning matters for privacy-sensitive applications

content.text: Federated learning addresses a genuine tension many organizations face: wanting to build a model that learns from data across multiple sources (multiple hospitals' patient data, multiple users' device data) while facing privacy regulations, competitive sensitivity, or contractual restrictions that prevent centralizing that raw data in one place. Because raw data never leaves its original location, federated learning can enable model training that would otherwise be legally or practically impossible due to data sharing restrictions, though it requires more sophisticated infrastructure than traditional centralized training.

items: Multiple sources — learn from data across organizations or devices.
Privacy regulations — compliance with data protection laws.
Competitive sensitivity — data stays within each organization.
Contractual restrictions — enables training where sharing is prohibited.
Infrastructure complexity — requires more than centralized training.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of federated learning

content.text: Federated learning has significant limitations. It requires more sophisticated infrastructure and coordination than centralized training. Model updates can theoretically leak information, and aggregation requires trust in the central server. Non-IID data distributions across participants can reduce model performance, and the approach requires participants to have sufficient compute resources. Federated learning is not a solution for every privacy-sensitive use case and may not be justified for smaller-scale applications where centralized training is possible.

items: Infrastructure complexity — more sophisticated than centralized training.
Privacy risk — model updates can theoretically leak some information.
Server trust — aggregation requires trust in the central server.
Non-IID data — data distributions across participants can reduce accuracy.
Compute requirements — participants need sufficient local resources.
Justification — not needed when centralized training is possible.

content.title: Important
content.text: Federated learning is powerful for privacy-sensitive distributed data, but it's complex and not always justified. Start with centralized training if possible.

content.text: Implementing federated learning effectively requires careful infrastructure design, participant coordination, and privacy considerations. The following practices can help ensure your federated learning project delivers value.

content.text: Measure the accuracy gap between federated and centralized training — if the gap is significant, federated learning may not be viable for your use case.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about federated learning

items.question: What's a real-world example of federated learning?
items.answer: Mobile keyboard prediction models that improve based on how users across many devices type, without any individual user's actual typed text being transmitted to a central server — only model improvement signals are shared.

items.question: Is federated learning relevant for a multi-hospital healthcare AI project?
items.answer: Yes, this is a common and valuable application — allowing model training across patient data from multiple healthcare institutions without any institution needing to share raw patient data with the others or a central party.

items.question: Does federated learning produce as accurate a model as centralized training?
items.answer: Often comparable, though some accuracy tradeoff can occur depending on data distribution across participants; ClickMasters validates this directly for your specific scenario rather than assuming parity.

items.question: Is federated learning more expensive than traditional centralized model training?
items.answer: Generally yes, given the added infrastructure complexity for distributed training coordination; ClickMasters only recommends it when genuine data centralization barriers justify this added cost.

items.question: How long does a federated learning project take?
items.answer: 16–36 weeks depending on the number of participants and infrastructure complexity, considerably longer than equivalent centralized training given the added coordination requirements.

items.question: Can federated learning be combined with additional privacy techniques like differential privacy?
items.answer: Yes, for use cases requiring stronger privacy guarantees than federated learning's basic architecture provides, ClickMasters can layer in additional techniques as part of the overall privacy strategy.

items.question: What is differential privacy and how does it relate to federated learning?
items.answer: Differential privacy adds controlled noise to data or model updates to prevent identifying individual data points. In federated learning, it can be applied to model updates before aggregation to provide stronger privacy guarantees against potential inference attacks.

items.question: What is non-IID data in federated learning?
items.answer: Non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) data means that each participant's local data distribution is different. This is common in real-world federated learning (e.g., user typing patterns vary) and can make training more challenging.

items.question: How does the central server aggregate model updates in federated learning?
items.answer: The most common method is FedAvg (Federated Averaging), which takes a weighted average of the model updates from participants. More sophisticated aggregation methods exist for handling varying participant data quality or size.

items.question: Can federated learning be used with deep learning models?
items.answer: Yes — federated learning can be applied to deep learning models, though communication costs for transmitting large model updates can be significant. Techniques like gradient compression and quantization can help reduce communication overhead.
